result: The manuscript provides background on Long QT syndrome (LQTS), the IKs channel structure and function, and the prevalence of LQTS-associated mutations. About 300 mutations in KCNQ1 and KCNE1 have been identified in LQTS patients, distributed throughout the channel sequence and likely causing dysfunction by different mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C1-C19 and C88-C94 establish well-documented background knowledge about LQTS, channel structure, and mutation prevalence, supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Hedley et al., 2009; Barhanin et al., 1996; Sanguinetti et al., 1996; Nerbonne and Kass, 2005; and others). This contextual information is appropriately referenced and consistent with the field.

result: All studied LQTS and LQTS-like mutations shift the G(V) of KV7.1+KCNE1 towards positive voltages and/or accelerate channel closing kinetics. The reduced current amplitudes in Xenopus oocytes are mainly attributed to gating defects rather than trafficking defects.
evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C20-C28 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements, and Supplementary file 1, showing consistent voltage-dependent and kinetic alterations across multiple mutants. The inference that gating defects (rather than trafficking) explain reduced currents (C27, C71) is reasonable given the correlation between observed and predicted current amplitudes, though the authors appropriately acknowledge that trafficking defects may contribute.

result: Heterozygous expression of mutant and wild-type subunits generally produces a milder biophysical phenotype compared to homozygous expression, consistent with clinical observations that heterozygous LQTS carriers have milder phenotypes than homozygous individuals.
evaluation: Claims C29-C30 and C77-C78 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2, showing that heterozygous expression produces more wild-type-like G(V), kinetics, and current amplitudes. The correlation with clinical phenotypes (C78) is appropriately supported by citations (Priori et al., 1998; Jackson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2008).

result: Voltage-clamp fluorometry experiments reveal that S225L and F351A mutations affect different gating transitions: S225L primarily interferes with the main voltage sensor (S4) movement, while F351A affects later gating transitions associated with pore opening. The LQTS mutant F351L shows similar properties to F351A.
evaluation: Claims C31-C41 and C72-C75 are supported by voltage-clamp fluorometry data in Figure 3 and kinetic modeling in Figure 3—figure supplements. The differential effects on F1 and F2 fluorescence components provide strong evidence for distinct molecular mechanisms. The authors appropriately note that their interpretation depends on the models used and that alternative mechanisms are possible. The F351L data (C75) provides additional validation for the F351A findings.

result: Similar mutation-induced alterations in IKs channel currents may be caused by different molecular mechanisms.
evaluation: Claim C4 is supported by the voltage-clamp fluorometry experiments (Figure 3) and kinetic modeling (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) showing that S225L and F351A produce similar shifts in G(V) but through different molecular mechanisms (affecting S4 movement vs. pore opening). This is a key integrative finding of the manuscript.

result: N-arachidonoyl taurine (N-AT) retains its ability to activate KV7.1 channels in the presence of KCNE1, unlike regular polyunsaturated fatty acids. N-AT is proposed to act by attracting the voltage sensor S4 through an electrostatic mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 and C83 are supported by prior work (Liin et al., 2015) and data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The proposed electrostatic mechanism (C83) is appropriately cited to previous work. This provides important context for the N-AT experiments on mutants.

result: N-AT restores channel gating of many different mutant channels across different domains and with different molecular defects. 70 µM N-AT shifts G(V) by 30-50 mV towards negative voltages, increases current amplitudes, speeds up opening kinetics, and slows closing kinetics for most mutants, effectively compensating for mutation-induced defects.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C45-C60, C79 are well-supported by extensive experimental data in Figure 4 and supplementary files showing consistent N-AT effects across multiple mutants with different locations and mechanisms. The quantitative measurements of voltage shifts, energy changes, current amplitudes, and kinetics are appropriately documented. The physiologically relevant pulsing protocol (C50-C52) strengthens the functional significance of the findings.

result: N-AT accelerates both the main gating charge movement (F1) and channel opening (F2) in mutant channels, as shown by voltage-clamp fluorometry. N-AT causes a dramatic decrease in fluorescence from Alexa488-labeled KV7.1/G219C*+KCNE1 channels, but this is not due to collisional quenching.
evaluation: Claims C61-C69 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplements. However, the dramatic fluorescence decrease caused by N-AT (C61) complicates interpretation, requiring normalization that introduces uncertainty. The authors acknowledge they cannot reliably quantify F2 for F351A+KCNE1 and cannot completely determine N-AT effects on F(V) of mutants. While the kinetic data (C66-C68) are more robust, the mechanistic interpretation (C69) remains somewhat uncertain due to these technical limitations.

result: N-AT is an interesting prototype compound for development of future IKs channel activators to treat LQTS caused by diverse mutations, as it shows general efficacy across mutants unlike previously reported KV7 channel activators that show variable sensitivity.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 and C96 represent appropriate conclusions based on the experimental findings. The comparison to other KV7 activators (C80) is supported by citations (Seebohm et al., 2003; Xiong et al., 2007; Leitner et al., 2012). The conclusion that N-AT is an interesting prototype (C81, C96) is justified by the data showing broad efficacy across mutants, though the authors appropriately frame this as a model compound requiring further development.

result: The manuscript provides additional context on trafficking defects in LQTS type 2, S4 movement during gating, potential mechanisms of N-AT action, current treatments for LQTS, and technical considerations for the experimental design.
evaluation: Claims C82, C84-C87, and C95 provide appropriate background and discussion context, supported by relevant citations. C85 is appropriately framed as a hypothesis based on analogy to hanatoxin. These claims support the interpretation and contextualization of the main findings.
